concepts.title: Events as Subsets of the Sample Space
concepts.definition: Once a random experiment lists every possible outcome as a sample space S, any chosen subset of S counts as an event. The event happens when the experiment's actual outcome lands inside that subset; getting exactly one head in two coin tosses is the subset {HT, TH} of S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}.
concepts.key_idea: Sample space is the universe of outcomes; an event is any subset of it, and it occurs when the realized outcome belongs to the subset.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh114.txt lines 15-70 (section 14.1 and 14.1.1 occurrence of an event, two coin toss sample space, subsets as events)
question_patterns: define an event in terms of the sample space

solution_steps.explain: Enumerate every outcome of the experiment -- for two coins that is HH, HT, TH, TT.
Collect the outcomes matching the event's description; this subset is the event.
The event occurs exactly when the observed outcome is one of the subset's elements.

concepts.title: Types of Events: Simple, Compound, Sure and Impossible
concepts.definition: Events come in types: a simple event holds exactly one sample point, a compound event holds two or more. The empty set is the impossible event (it can never happen), the full sample space is the sure event (it always happens), and elementary events are the single-outcome atoms that build everything else.
concepts.key_idea: One outcome = simple; many outcomes = compound; empty = impossible; the whole space = sure.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh114.txt lines 71-140 (section 14.1.2 types of events, impossible and sure events, simple and compound events)
question_patterns: classify the given events as simple or compound

in class 11 probability: what is a sure event
distinguish an elementary event from a compound event
why does the empty set represent an impossible event
give an example of a compound event in a die experiment

solution_steps.explain: Check how many outcomes of S the event contains.
Exactly one point makes it simple (elementary); more than one makes it compound.
The empty subset can contain no outcome, so it is impossible; S itself contains every outcome, so it is sure.

concepts.title: Mutually Exclusive and Exhaustive Events
concepts.definition: Events are mutually exclusive when no outcome belongs to two of them at once, so they cannot both fire in one run of the experiment. They are exhaustive when together they cover every outcome of the sample space. In a die roll, the events 'even number' and 'odd number' are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
concepts.key_idea: Exclusive means disjoint subsets; exhaustive means their union is the whole sample space -- a set-theoretic double test.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh114.txt lines 141-220 (sections 14.1.3 algebra of events, 14.1.4 mutually exclusive, 14.1.5 exhaustive events, die examples)
question_patterns: determine whether two given events are mutually exclusive
when do events form an exhaustive system
in class 11 probability: can two mutually exclusive events occur together
check whether the given events are exhaustive as well as exclusive
give a die example of mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
how does the union of exhaustive events relate to the sample space

solution_steps.explain: If the common outcomes are none, the events are mutually exclusive.
If the union equals the full sample space, the events are exhaustive.
Both tests are independent -- a family can be exclusive, exhaustive, both or neither.

concepts.title: Probability of Equally Likely Outcomes
concepts.definition: When every outcome of the sample space is equally likely, the probability of an event is the count of outcomes favourable to it divided by the total count of outcomes in S. This ratio always sits between 0 and 1, hitting 0 for impossible events and 1 for sure ones.
concepts.key_idea: Favourable over total -- the classical probability ratio for symmetric experiments like dice, coins and cards.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh114.txt lines 221-300 (sections 14.2, 14.2.1, 14.2.2 axiomatic approach, probabilities of equally likely outcomes, bounds 0 to 1)

solution_steps.explain: List the subset of S matching the event and count its size.
The ratio of favourable outcomes to all outcomes is the event's probability.

concepts.title: Probability of the Event 'A or B'
concepts.definition: For events A and B, the chance that at least one occurs is P(A) plus P(B) minus P(A and B); the subtraction removes the overlap that would otherwise be counted twice. When A and B are mutually exclusive the overlap term is zero and the probabilities simply add.
concepts.key_idea: Add the two chances, then pay back the double-counted overlap -- or skip the payback when the events cannot coincide.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh114.txt lines 301-380 (section 14.2.3 probability of the event 'A or B', addition theorem, mutually exclusive case)
question_patterns: find the probability that event A or event B occurs

in class 11 probability: state the addition rule for two events

solution_steps.explain: P(A) + P(B) counts every shared outcome twice.
Subtracting P(A and B) leaves each outcome counted exactly once.

concepts.title: Probability of the Event 'Not A' (Complement)
concepts.definition: The complement of event A, written 'not A', gathers every sample point outside A; its probability is one minus the probability of A. Since A and its complement are mutually exclusive and together exhaustive, their probabilities must total exactly 1.
concepts.key_idea: Whatever the event does not take, the complement takes -- so the two probabilities split the whole 1 between them.
concepts.textbook_ref: kemh114.txt lines 381-450 (section 14.2.4 probability of the event 'not A', complement rule, P(A) + P(not A) = 1)
question_patterns: find the probability that event A does not occur

in class 11 probability: why must P(A) plus P(not A) equal 1

what is the probability of not drawing a king from a deck
use the complement rule to avoid counting many cases

solution_steps.explain: The complement rule converts 'not A' into a single subtraction.
